H0 (Null Hypothesis): Energy consumption distributions are identical on weekdays and weekends
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): Energy consumption differs significantly between weekdays and weekends
Plain-English Interpretation: Statistically significant (p < 0.001). Weekend mean (100.6 Wh) is slightly higher than weekday mean (96.6 Wh). Effect size is small (Cohen's d = 0.039), reflecting higher weekend residential activity.

H0 (Null Hypothesis): Daytime and nighttime energy consumption distributions are equal
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): Daytime energy consumption is significantly greater than nighttime
Plain-English Interpretation: Highly significant (p < 0.001). Daytime mean (119.7 Wh) is more than double nighttime mean (53.7 Wh). Moderate-to-large effect size (d = 0.675), confirming baseline standby sleep vs active waking consumption.

H0 (Null Hypothesis): Appliance consumption is identical whether lights are on or off
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): Appliance consumption is significantly higher when lights are on
Plain-English Interpretation: Extremely significant (p < 0.001). When lights are active, mean appliance energy is 135.5 Wh vs 86.6 Wh when lights are off (d = 0.487). Lighting serves as a strong proxy for active human occupancy.

H0 (Null Hypothesis): No correlation between outdoor temperature and appliance energy (r = 0)
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): Significant linear or monotonic correlation between T_out and Appliances
Plain-English Interpretation: Statistically significant (p < 0.001), but very weak linear association (Pearson r = 0.099, Spearman rho = 0.216). Outdoor temperature alone does not explain appliance load spikes, which are driven by occupant behavior.

H0 (Null Hypothesis): Appliance energy consumption distributions are equal across all months
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): At least one month differs significantly in energy consumption
Plain-English Interpretation: Statistically significant differences across months (H = 492.92, p < 0.001), but negligible effect size (epsilon-sq = 0.0248, eta-sq = 0.0005). Month-to-month baseline appliance consumption remains steady around ~95-101 Wh on average.

Hypothesis Topic: Time of Day vs High Usage Event
H0 (Null Hypothesis): High-usage intervals (>100 Wh) occur independently of the time of day
H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): High-usage intervals are significantly dependent on the time of day
Plain-English Interpretation: Extremely strong dependency between Time of Day and High Usage (Chi2 = 2072.6, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.324). High-demand spikes (>100 Wh) cluster heavily in Evening and Afternoon hours compared to quiet Night hours.
